The declines came as investors grew increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending In this article 9984.T-JP TSM ASM-NL NVDA SKHY ASML CRWV INTC NOK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:29 03:29 Derek Yan: The AI investment cycle is far from slowing down Morning Call Nvidia , Micron and AMD sank on Thursday, as stocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade across the globe continued to plummet. Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment. Nvidia fell about 2.5%, Micron sank about 3.5% and AMD lost 6%. Neoclouds also dropped, with CoreWeave sank 10%, Nebius lost nearly 8% and IREN fell 12%. Intel lost about 6.5%. A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday. South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%. In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%. Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML was last down 5.2%, Infineon Technologies shed 8.2% and ASM International was down 8.6%. Why stocks are selling off The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom. Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028." Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%. watch now VIDEO 6:59 06:59 Kospi on track for weakest close since April as global AI sell-off deepens Squawk Box Europe Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust. "Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note. The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs. headlines.article_text: Amazon launches Bee Frontier and Eclipse AI devices Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon is releasing two new Bee listening devices as it moves further into the AI hardware market. The $75 Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of its wearable bracelet, while the $100 Bee Eclipse attaches to a user's smartphone. It marks the first update to the Bee lineup since Amazon acquired the startup in July 2025. Amazon Amazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market. The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor. Amazon acquired Bee , a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations. The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post. Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said. Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware . Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets , while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia -powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI. The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market. The $100 Bee Eclipse is a credit card-sized device that magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. Meta has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers. Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace. Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word. When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions. With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps. The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said. An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said. Merck CEO tells CNBC he expects breakthrough cancer vaccine will become faster to make
headlines.summary: His comments come after Merck officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility in the Greater Philadelphia area.
headlines.article_text: Merck CEO: Cancer vaccine manufacturing time could shrink Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Merck CEO Rob Davis told CNBC that he expects the company's breakthrough cancer vaccine with Moderna to get faster to make over time. Davis acknowledged that manufacturing the vaccine is a "complex system," but said Merck and Moderna have the process "down to a very tight science." His comments came after Merck on Wednesday officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility in the Greater Philadelphia area. In this article MRK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:45 03:45 Merck CEO Davis on new manufacturing site: Will meaningfully accelerate getting drugs to patients Squawk on the Street Merck CEO Rob Davis told CNBC on Wednesday that he expects the company's breakthrough cancer vaccine with Moderna to get faster to manufacture over time. Shortening the current six-week timeline could potentially help the companies reach more patients. "We are going to drive for improvement, but right now the focus really is, let's make sure we have the supply ready, we have the market ready to bring this important innovation to the market, and then we'll talk about how do we accelerate," he told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "But I do think over time you're going to see that timeline shortened." The personalized cancer vaccine turnaround spans from sequencing a patient's tumor to delivering it to the hospital. Merck and Moderna's vaccine is designed to target the specific mutations in each individual patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach, which makes it complicated to produce. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Merck's blockbuster immunotherapy Keytruda, which aims to help the body attack the cancer more effectively. Davis acknowledged that manufacturing the vaccine is a "complex system," but said Merck and Moderna have the process "down to a very tight science." "I'm actually very confident that we're not going to have complexities in getting this to patients in a very timely fashion," he added. "We're doing it in our clinicals, and I only see improvement going forward." His comments come after the two companies in August released positive initial data from a late-stage trial on the shot in combination with Keytruda in melanoma patients. Davis said the company is also examining the vaccine in trials across other tumors, including non-small cell lung cancer, types of bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. "You like to talk that maybe you can start moving toward talking about a cure," he said. "We're not there yet, but we're moving in a direction with technology that's really unprecedented." Merck's new R&D facility Davis spoke to CNBC after Merck earlier Wednesday officially opened its new 120,000-square-foot research facility , which it has named Advance, in its West Point, Pennsylvania, campus. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro joined Merck executives and other government officials for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to celebrate the launch of the facility, which features highly automated robotic systems and advanced digital AI capabilities. Merck says the facility is designed to streamline the analysis of biological samples from the company's ongoing drug programs and improve its research and development. The opening of the new facility comes as Merck prepares for the upcoming loss of exclusivity of Keytruda, which is one of the world's top-selling drugs and is widely viewed as the backbone of modern cancer treatment. Keytruda's core U.S. compound patent expires in December 2028, while secondary patents extend protection into 2029 and beyond. Merck has implemented a multi-layered strategy to turn the Keytruda transition into what it views as a manageable "hill" rather than a sharp revenue cliff. That includes accelerating internal research and also funneling $65 billion in external acquisitions and licensing agreements over the five years to build its pipeline of next-generation medicines. Robert Davis, CEO of Merck, testifies before the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee at the Dirksen Senate Office Building on February 08, 2024 in Washington, DC. Kevin Dietsch | Getty Images News | Getty Images The pharmaceutical giant is also developing new forms of Keytruda and combination regimens that it can transition patients onto and protect the drug's revenue even after key patents expire before 2030. The Food and Drug Administration in September 2025 approved the subcutaneous form of Keytruda, which is considered a more convenient version because it is administered under the skin in minutes. The standard form of the drug is an intravenous infusion that takes around 30 minutes. But Merck is facing a legal battle over the newer version in some European markets, raising questions about the market size for the drug. A Dutch court issued an injunction earlier this month blocking Merck from selling, stocking or manufacturing subcutaneous Keytruda across eight European countries: Belgium, Denmark, France, Ireland, Italy, Sweden, Switzerland and the Netherlands. That followed a patent infringement suit brought by the biotech company Halozyme Therapeutics over its own subcutaneous drug delivery platform. Merck has said it strongly disagrees with the rulings and plans to appeal. Patients can still receive the original form of Keytruda in Europe while the patent dispute unfolds. Still, Halozyme has also sued Merck for patent infringement ​in ⁠the U.S., alleging the subcutaneous formulation of Keytruda infringes 15 patents that the biotech has filed since 2011. Meanwhile, Merck is focused on rolling out a slate of new drugs. That includes Winrevair, a treatment for a rare, life-threatening lung disease that was approved in 2024 and acquired a few years earlier through its $11.5 billion acquisition of Acceleron . Another closely watched launch is Merck's cholesterol-lowering pill Lipfendra, which was approved by the FDA in July.
